desc:
Given an array nums of non-negative integers, count the ordered triples of indices (i, j, k) such that nums[i] & nums[j] & nums[k] == 0, where & is the bitwise AND.

The indices need not be distinct: (0, 0, 0) is a valid triple whenever nums[0] == 0, and (i, j, k) and (j, i, k) count separately.

For example, nums = [2, 1, 3] gives 12.
constraints: The answer is at most 700<sup>3</sup>, which fits in 32 bits
hints: There are n<sup>3</sup> triples, up to 343 million. Can you handle the first two indices together and the third one separately?
Count how many ordered pairs (i, j) produce each possible AND value x = nums[i] & nums[j]. There are only 4,096 possible values of x.

For a third element v you need the number of pairs whose AND has no bit in common with v, i.e. whose AND is a subset of the mask ~v (within 12 bits). A subset-sum (zeta) transform over the 12 bits precomputes that count for every mask.
editorial: First collect pair[x], the number of ordered pairs (i, j) with nums[i] & nums[j] = x. Looping over distinct values with their multiplicities keeps this at about d2 steps for d distinct values, instead of n2 pair visits.

A triple is good exactly when x & v = 0, i.e. when every set bit of x lies in the complement mask m = ~v & 4095, so x is a submask of m. Define sub[m] as the sum of pair[x] over all submasks x of m; the standard way is a loop over each bit b doing sub[m] += sub[m ^ (1 << b)] for masks containing b, which takes 12 · 4096 steps. The answer is the sum over elements v of sub[~v & 4095].
Total time is O(d<sup>2</sup> + B · 2<sup>B</sup>) with B = 12 bits, versus O(n<sup>3</sup>) for the direct count.
